kurals.tamil:
பொருளல்ல வற்றைப் பொருளென்று உணரும்
மருளானாம் மாணாப் பிறப்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Porulalla vatraip porulendru unarum
Marulaanaam maanaap pirappu.
kurals.meaning: Taking things that are not real to be the real thing is a delusion, and it is from this delusion that a birth without dignity arises: the endless round of lowly rebirths.
kurals.elementary: Imagine chasing a shiny puddle on a hot road, sure it’s water, when it’s only a mirage. You’d run and run, get more and more thirsty, and never drink. This kural says that when we treat things that don’t last as if they were the real treasure, we keep chasing mirages again and again, life after life.
kurals.university: The chapter opens with a diagnosis rather than a prescription: the root of bondage is marul (delusion, confusion), specifically the cognitive error of taking porul-alladhu (what is not the real) for porul (the real). Commentators such as Parimelazhagar read maanaa-p-pirappu (‘inglorious birth’) as the whole cycle of transmigration, which turns the couplet into an epistemological account of samsara: rebirth is caused less by particular sins than by misperception. This closely matches the Advaita Vedanta analysis of adhyasa (superimposition, the classic rope mistaken for a snake) and the Buddhist teaching that avijja (ignorance) is the first link of dependent origination. Because the Tamil ‘porul’ is richly ambiguous (thing, wealth, meaning, reality), the couplet also carries an ethical undertone: whoever treats wealth and possessions as the ultimate ‘thing’ has mistaken the counterfeit for the coin.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “From the unreal lead me to the real! From the darkness lead me to the light! From death lead me to immortality!”
hinduism.explanation: This ancient Upanishadic prayer asks to be led away from what is unreal toward what is truly real. The Upanishad itself explains that the ‘unreal’ and ‘darkness’ mean death, and the ‘real’ and ‘light’ mean immortality.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar names the same wrong turn (taking the unreal for the real) and the same cost: being caught in death and birth again and again.
hinduism.source: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.3.28 (Pavamana Mantra), trans. Patrick Olivelle
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match: the unreal/real contrast is tied explicitly to death vs. immortality. Translations of ‘asat’ vary (Madhavananda renders it ‘evil’); Olivelle’s wording verified as cited on Wikipedia.

christianity.quote_or_event: “While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells Christians not to fix their eyes on visible things, which pass away, but on unseen realities, which last forever.
christianity.tie_back: Same distinction the Kural draws between passing things wrongly treated as ‘real’ and the lasting reality; the Kural adds rebirth as the consequence of getting it wrong.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on temporal vs. eternal reality; no concept of rebirth, and the ‘error’ is framed as a matter of focus rather than delusion.

islam.quote_or_event: “Know that the life of this world is but amusement and diversion and adornment and boasting to one another and competition in increase of wealth and children … And what is the worldly life except the enjoyment of delusion.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes worldly life as a passing show, like a plant that flourishes after rain and then dries into debris, and calls its enjoyment ‘delusion’.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘marul’ (delusion) and the Qur’an’s ‘enjoyment of delusion’ both describe treating the fleeting world as the real prize.
islam._accuracy_note: Close thematic and lexical match (‘delusion’); the consequence is accountability in the Hereafter, not rebirth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.”
judaism.explanation: The Hebrew word translated ‘vanity’ (hevel) literally means vapor or breath. Ecclesiastes says that what people chase as solid and lasting is really as thin as breath.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Ecclesiastes warns that what looks substantial is not the real thing; unlike the Kural, it does not tie this mistake to rebirth.
judaism._accuracy_note: Captures the ‘unreal treated as real’ theme; lacks the causal link to rebirth and the positive knowledge of truth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Those who mistake the unessential to be essential and the essential to be unessential, dwelling in wrong thoughts, never arrive at the essential.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that people who confuse the worthless with the valuable, and the valuable with the worthless, are stuck in wrong thinking and never reach what truly matters.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost the same sentence as the Kural: mistaking the non-essential for the essential is the error that keeps beings in bondage.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one structural match (not-X taken as X); rebirth is implicit in the wider Buddhist framework rather than stated in the verse.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ixion, invited to dine among the gods, desired Hera. Zeus shaped a cloud (Nephele) into Hera’s likeness; Ixion embraced the phantom as if it were real and was punished by being bound to an ever-turning wheel.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ixion fell for an illusion made to look like the real thing, and his punishment was an endless, spinning wheel.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s picture of mistaking a phantom for reality and being trapped in an endless cycle is strikingly mirrored in Ixion’s cloud and wheel.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Vivid imagery match (illusion → endless wheel), but the myth’s moral is chiefly about ingratitude and hubris, not metaphysical ignorance.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “To them, I said, the truth would be literally nothing but the shadows of the images.”
philosophy.explanation: In Plato’s Allegory of the Cave, prisoners chained since birth see only shadows on a wall and take them for the whole of reality.
philosophy.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s diagnosis: people take what is not real (shadows) for the real, and that mistake defines the whole condition they live in.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on unreal-taken-as-real; Plato frames the consequence as imprisonment in ignorance rather than rebirth (though Republic X does include a rebirth myth).

kurals.tamil:
இருள்நீங்கி இன்பம் பயக்கும் மருள்நீங்கி
மாசறு காட்சி யவர்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Irulneengi inbam payakkum marulneengi
Maasaru kaatchi yavarkku.
kurals.meaning: For those who have left delusion behind and gained a clear, flawless vision of the truth, that vision drives away the darkness and brings true bliss.
kurals.elementary: When you switch on the light in a dark room, the scary shape in the corner turns out to be just a coat on a chair, and suddenly you feel safe and happy. People who see the truth clearly are like that: the light of truth chases away the darkness and fear, and joy comes in.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on a matched pair: irul neengi (darkness departs) and marul neengi (delusion departs). When inner confusion (marul) is removed, outer darkness (irul, which commentators gloss as the darkness of hell or of future births) also lifts. The key phrase maasaru kaatchi, ‘stainless seeing’, frames liberation as a kind of vision (compare the Sanskrit darshana) rather than mere intellectual agreement, and Parimelazhagar takes the resulting inbam (bliss) as the bliss of release (veedu). The light/darkness metaphor for knowledge and ignorance is shared with the Upanishads (tamaso ma jyotir gamaya), with the Buddha’s first sermon (‘illumination arose’), and with Plato’s ascent from the cave. What stands out in Valluvar is the ethical precondition built into the seeing itself: the vision must be free of stain (maasu).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When, however, one is enlightened with the knowledge by which nescience is destroyed, then his knowledge reveals everything, as the sun lights up everything in the daytime.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna compares true knowledge to the rising sun: once ignorance is destroyed, everything is seen clearly, as objects become visible at dawn.
hinduism.tie_back: Same movement as the Kural: when ignorance (marul) is removed, darkness (irul) goes and clear vision takes its place.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-direct match of knowledge dispelling ignorance like light dispelling darkness; bliss is implied in context rather than stated in this verse.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.”
christianity.explanation: In the Beatitudes, Jesus promises that people whose hearts are pure and undivided will see God.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘maasaru kaatchi’ (stainless seeing) and ‘inbam’ (bliss) match the Beatitude’s purity, seeing, and blessedness almost exactly.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on purity → vision → blessedness; the object seen is a personal God rather than ‘the true nature of things’.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allāh is the Ally of those who believe. He brings them out from darknesses into the light.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes God leading believers out of layers of darkness into light, while false guides lead people the other way.
islam.tie_back: The same passage from darkness to light that the Kural promises to those freed from delusion.
islam._accuracy_note: Good imagery match; in the Qur’an the agent is God’s guidance, whereas the Kural emphasizes the seeker’s own purified insight.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For with thee is the fountain of life: in thy light shall we see light.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist says that true sight is only possible within God’s own light, which is also the source of life.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Psalm links clear seeing, light, and the fullness of life.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good imagery overlap (light, seeing, life); no explicit theme of removing delusion.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Vision arose, insight arose, discernment arose, knowledge arose, illumination arose within me with regard to things never heard before: ‘This is the noble truth of stress.’”
buddhism.explanation: In his first sermon the Buddha describes his awakening to the Four Noble Truths as vision and illumination, ending with the certainty that there would be no further birth.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘stainless seeing’ that removes darkness corresponds to the Buddha’s ‘vision… illumination’; both ground liberation in seeing truth directly.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 56.11, Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match: liberation as vision/illumination; the same sutta also speaks of the Dhamma eye as ‘dustless, stainless’, echoing ‘maasaru’.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Homeric Hymn to Demeter closes by declaring blessed the person on earth who has seen the Eleusinian Mysteries, while the uninitiated has no such good lot after death, down in the darkness and gloom.
greek_mythology.explanation: Initiates at Eleusis were promised a happier fate after death because of what they had ‘seen’ in the secret rites.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, a saving ‘sight’ separates those who reach bliss from those left in darkness.
greek_mythology.source: Homeric Hymn to Demeter, lines c. 480–482
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. The ‘seeing’ is ritual initiation rather than philosophical insight into reality.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The instrument of knowledge can only by the movement of the whole soul be turned from the world of becoming into that of being, and learn by degrees to endure the sight of being, and of the brightest and best of being, or in other words, of the good.”
philosophy.explanation: Plato says education is not putting sight into blind eyes but turning the whole soul away from shifting appearances toward true being, which it learns to look at directly.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘marul neengi… maasaru kaatchi’ (delusion gone, pure vision gained) is Plato’s turn from becoming to being, from shadow to light.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on the turn from illusion to the vision of reality; Plato’s endpoint is ‘the Good’, not release from rebirth.

kurals.tamil:
ஐயத்தின் நீங்கித் தெளிந்தார்க்கு வையத்தின்
வானம் நணிய துடைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Aiyaththin neengith thelindhaarkku vaiyaththin
Vaanam naniya thudaiththu.
kurals.meaning: For those who have moved beyond doubt and reached clear certainty, heaven is nearer than the very earth they stand on.
kurals.elementary: When you’re not sure which path leads home, even a short walk feels long and scary. But once you know the way for certain, home feels close. This kural says that people who have cleared away all doubt about what is true feel heaven is closer to them than the ground under their feet.
kurals.university: Aiyam (doubt) is here a technical term: Indian epistemology treats samshaya (doubt) as one of the defects of cognition that block liberation, alongside viparyaya (error), which Kural 351 addressed. Thelivu (clarity, settled understanding) is the positive term, and Valluvar’s hyperbole (vaanam naniyadhu, ‘the sky/heaven is nearer’) turns ordinary spatial logic upside down: the earth we stand on becomes the distant, precarious thing, while the spiritual goal becomes immediate. Commentators take vaanam as the higher world or liberation (veedu). The inversion echoes the Gita’s warning that the doubting soul finds happiness neither here nor hereafter, and the Mundaka Upanishad’s ‘all doubts are solved’ when the Real is seen. Comparative readers may also note Deuteronomy’s insistence that the divine word is ‘not in heaven’ but ‘very nigh unto thee’, a similar collapsing of distance, though grounded in revelation rather than insight.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “But ignorant and faithless persons who doubt the revealed scriptures do not attain God consciousness. For the doubting soul there is happiness neither in this world nor in the next.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns that a mind stuck in doubt gains nothing, neither happiness in this life nor in the next.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the mirror image of the Kural: doubt closes off both worlds, while freedom from doubt brings heaven closer than earth.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Inverse but precise match (doubt vs. certainty and the higher world). The Gita stresses faith in scripture, while the Kural stresses clarity of understanding.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Neither shall they say, Lo here! or, lo there! for, behold, the kingdom of God is within you.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells people not to look for God’s kingdom as some distant place or future event: it is already present, within or among them.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it collapses the distance to ‘heaven’: for the one who understands, it is nearer than anything outside.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the nearness-of-heaven idea; says nothing specifically about overcoming doubt.

islam.quote_or_event: “And We have already created man and know what his soul whispers to him, and We are closer to him than [his] jugular vein.”
islam.explanation: God declares that He is nearer to each person than their own jugular vein. Islamic spirituality pairs this nearness with yaqin, firm certainty, as the state in which that nearness is actually known.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘heaven is nearer than earth’ finds a strong echo in God being nearer than one’s own vein.
islam._accuracy_note: Nearness theme matches well; the doubt/certainty element is supplied by the wider concept of yaqin, not by this verse.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it.”
judaism.explanation: Moses tells Israel that God’s teaching is ‘not in heaven’ or beyond the sea, where someone would have to fetch it, but very near, in their own mouth and heart.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts remove the imagined distance between a person and the highest truth.
judaism._accuracy_note: Parallel collapse of distance; the Jewish text concerns accessibility of commandment, not freedom from doubt.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Better than sole sovereignty over the earth, better than going to heaven, better even than lordship over all the worlds is the supramundane Fruition of Stream Entrance.”
buddhism.explanation: Stream-entry, the first stage of awakening, is reached partly by abandoning doubt (vicikiccha), one of the first three fetters. The Dhammapada says this attainment is worth more than ruling the earth or going to heaven.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the one freed from doubt gains something that outranks all earthly possession.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Doctrinally close (stream-entry entails the end of doubt); the verse itself does not name doubt.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The sea-god Proteus foretells that Menelaus will not die in Argos, but the gods will carry him to the Elysian plain at the ends of the earth, where life is easiest for men.
greek_mythology.explanation: Elysium is a paradise where a favored few go instead of the gloomy underworld.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A heavenly destination opened to a few, but it is not reached through freedom from doubt.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weak match. Menelaus earns Elysium through his marriage to Helen (a daughter of Zeus), not through knowledge or certainty; included as the nearest Greek ‘heaven’ image.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Boethius’s Consolation of Philosophy, Lady Philosophy finds the imprisoned narrator’s mind clouded by confusion. She wipes his eyes, the night is scattered, and he recognizes her; she then leads him by argument from doubt to settled insight.
philosophy.explanation: Philosophy cures the narrator’s blindness and confusion step by step until he sees his true situation clearly.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘aiyaththin neengi thelindhaar’ (those who have left doubt and become clear) describes exactly the journey Boethius dramatizes.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book I
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Good match on doubt → clarity; the ‘nearness of heaven’ element is only implicit in Boethius’s later books.

kurals.tamil:
ஐயுணர்வு எய்தியக் கண்ணும் பயமின்றே
மெய்யுணர்வு இல்லா தவர்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Aiyunarvu eydhiyak kannum payamindre
Meyyunarvu illaa thavarkku.
kurals.meaning: Even if someone has fully mastered all that the five senses can know, it brings no real benefit if they lack true knowledge of reality.
kurals.elementary: A person could have perfect eyes, sharp ears and a great nose, and still walk right past a treasure because they don’t know what it is. This kural says the five senses are like a camera: very useful, but you need a wise mind to understand what the pictures really mean.
kurals.university: Aiyunarvu, ‘five-fold awareness’, has two classical readings, both preserved in the commentary tradition. Mu. Varadarasanar and others take it as the complete knowledge gathered through the five senses, while Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it as the ascetic’s mastery or restraint of the five senses. Either way the claim is striking: neither sensory knowledge nor sensory discipline is enough without meyyunarvu, knowledge of the real. The second reading turns the couplet into a pointed warning to renunciants (the chapter sits in the Thuravaraviyal, the section on the ascetic life) that austerity without insight is barren. Philosophically it anticipates the argument of Plato’s Theaetetus that knowledge cannot simply be perception, and it parallels Heraclitus’s remark that eyes and ears are bad witnesses for souls that cannot interpret them.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “But, Sir, with all this I know the Mantras only, the sacred books, I do not know the Self. I have heard from men like you, that he who knows the Self overcomes grief.”
hinduism.explanation: The sage Narada lists every science he has mastered (the Vedas, grammar, logic, astronomy, the arts) and then admits to his teacher that he still does not know the Self and is in grief.
hinduism.tie_back: The same point as the Kural: vast learning and perception bring no real benefit without knowledge of the ultimate truth.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close in spirit (all learning is ‘only a name’ without Self-knowledge); concerns scriptural learning rather than the five senses.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore speak I to them in parables: because they seeing see not; and hearing they hear not, neither do they understand.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says many people have working eyes and ears but miss the meaning of what they see and hear.
christianity.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s paradox: full use of the senses, yet no real perception of truth.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on senses without understanding; the context is spiritual receptivity to Jesus’s teaching.

islam.quote_or_event: “They have hearts with which they do not understand, they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear. Those are like livestock; rather, they are more astray.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes people who have every faculty of perception but fail to grasp the truth, so their senses bring them no benefit.
islam.tie_back: Nearly identical to the Kural: complete sensory equipment is useless without true understanding.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close match on faculties without insight; the Qur’an adds a strong note of moral heedlessness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hear now this, O foolish people, and without understanding; which have eyes, and see not; which have ears, and hear not.”
judaism.explanation: The prophet Jeremiah rebukes people who have functioning senses but no understanding of God and of what is right.
judaism.tie_back: The same contrast the Kural draws between sensory capacity and true knowing.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong verbal match; the prophetic context is covenant faithfulness rather than metaphysical insight.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Much though he recites the sacred texts, but acts not accordingly, that heedless man is like a cowherd who only counts the cows of others — he does not partake of the blessings of the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares a person who knows many texts but doesn’t realize them to a herdsman counting cows that belong to someone else.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, accumulated knowledge without realization of truth yields no real benefit.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on ‘knowledge without realization is fruitless’; the verse concerns textual learning, not the five senses.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Oedipus legend, the blind seer Tiresias knows the terrible truth, while King Oedipus, clear-sighted and famous for solving the Sphinx’s riddle, cannot see his own situation. When the truth finally comes out, Oedipus blinds himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth deliberately flips sight and insight: the man with perfect eyes is blind to reality, and the blind man sees it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A dramatic illustration of the Kural: perfect senses bring no benefit without perception of the truth.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the play’s central irony; the truth at stake is personal and tragic rather than cosmic.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Eyes and ears are bad witnesses to men if they have souls that understand not their language.”
philosophy.explanation: Heraclitus says the senses only report; without a soul able to interpret them, their testimony misleads.
philosophy.tie_back: A near-exact philosophical restatement of the Kural: sense-knowledge is worthless without understanding of the real.
philosophy.source: Heraclitus, Fragment 107 (DK B107; trans. John Burnet)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very strong match; Heraclitus’s ‘Logos’ plays the role of the Kural’s ‘meypporul’.

kurals.tamil:
எப்பொருள் எத்தன்மைத் தாயினும் அப்பொருள்
மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்பது அறிவு.
kurals.transliteration:
Epporul eththanmaith thaayinum apporul
Meypporul kaanpadhu arivu.
kurals.meaning: Whatever a thing may be, and however it may appear, wisdom is seeing the true reality within that thing.
kurals.elementary: Two chocolates can look exactly the same, but one might have caramel inside and the other a nut. You only know by looking inside. This kural says a wise person doesn’t stop at how things look on the outside but finds out what they really are.
kurals.university: This is the chapter’s most quoted couplet, and it works as a definition: arivu (wisdom) is meypporul kaanpadhu, ‘seeing the true thing’ in every porul, whatever its apparent nature (eththanmaith thaayinum). The chain of repetitions (epporul, apporul, meypporul) performs the act it describes, peeling ‘thing’ back to ‘true thing’. Mu. Varadarasanar’s gloss makes the point explicit: one must not be dazzled by how a thing appears but know its real nature. Modern readers often extend it to critical thinking in general, meaning not being taken in by surface, reputation, or rhetoric. The ideal is close to the Buddhist yathabhuta-ñanadassana (‘knowing and seeing things as they really are’) and to the Greek project, from Heraclitus to Plato, of distinguishing a thing’s real nature (phusis) from how it seems (doxa).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The door of the True is covered with a golden disk. Open that, O Pûshan, that we may see the nature of the True.”
hinduism.explanation: The seeker prays that the dazzling golden covering over reality be removed so that the truth behind it can be seen.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s demand to look past a thing’s appearance to its ‘meypporul’ matches the prayer to remove the golden lid and see the True.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong image match (attractive surface hiding the Real); the Upanishad concerns ultimate Truth, the Kural every object.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his critics not to judge by surface impressions but by what is truly right.
christianity.tie_back: Same principle as the Kural: see through appearance to reality.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on appearance vs. reality; framed as moral judgment rather than metaphysical insight.

islam.quote_or_event: “But perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you; and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. And Allāh knows, while you know not.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an reminds believers that how something seems to them can be the opposite of what it really is; only God knows its true nature.
islam.tie_back: Both texts insist that a thing’s appearance can mislead and its true nature must be sought.
islam._accuracy_note: Good principle-level match; the verse’s immediate context is the obligation to fight, and final knowledge is reserved to God.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.”
judaism.explanation: When Samuel is about to anoint the impressive-looking Eliab, God tells him that outward appearance is not the measure: God sees the inner reality.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural asks human wisdom to see as God sees here, past the outward form to the true substance.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on outward form vs. inner reality.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “‘All conditioned things are impermanent’ — when one sees this with wisdom, one turns away from suffering. This is the path to purification.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that wisdom means seeing the real characteristics of things (impermanent, unsatisfactory, not-self) behind their seeming permanence. The tradition calls this yathabhuta, seeing things as they really are.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘meypporul kaanpadhu arivu’ is essentially the Buddhist definition of wisdom as seeing things as they truly are.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close in method; Buddhism specifies the three marks as the ‘true nature’, where the Kural leaves it open.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: To learn the truth, Menelaus must seize the shape-shifting sea-god Proteus and hold on while he turns into a lion, a serpent, a leopard, a boar, running water and a tree. Only when Proteus returns to his own form does he speak truly.
greek_mythology.explanation: The truth is available only to the one who refuses to be fooled by changing appearances and holds on until the real form shows itself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A perfect myth of the Kural’s teaching: whatever form a thing takes, wisdom grasps its true nature.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong allegorical match, though in Homer it is a literal episode, not a stated teaching.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For, though all things come to pass in accordance with this Word, men seem as if they had no experience of them, when they make trial of words and deeds such as I set forth, dividing each thing according to its kind and showing how it truly is.”
philosophy.explanation: Heraclitus describes his philosophical task as showing ‘how each thing truly is’, something most people miss even though it is all around them. (He also says, in Fragment 123, that ‘Nature loves to hide.’)
philosophy.tie_back: Heraclitus’s aim of showing ‘how it truly is’ is the Kural’s ‘meypporul kaanpadhu’ almost word for word.
philosophy.source: Heraclitus, Fragment 1 (DK B1; trans. John Burnet)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on the task of seeing each thing’s true nature.

kurals.tamil:
கற்றீண்டு மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டார் தலைப்படுவர்
மற்றீண்டு வாரா நெறி.
kurals.transliteration:
Katreendu meypporul kandaar thalaippaduvar
Matreendu vaaraa neri.
kurals.meaning: Those who have learned, and here in this very life have seen the True Reality, set out on the path that never returns here again.
kurals.elementary: When you finally solve a really hard maze, you don’t have to go back into it: you’ve found the way out. This kural says that people who learn deeply and truly understand what is real find the way out of the maze of being born again and again.
kurals.university: Two emphases distinguish this couplet: kattru (having learned) and eendu (here, in this very life). Valluvar insists that realization must happen within embodied existence, a ‘liberation while living’ close to the Vedantic jivanmukti and to the Buddhist arahant who knows ‘this is the last birth’. Learning is the necessary first step, but the verb is kandaar (they saw), not merely ‘they studied’: scholarship must end in direct seeing, and Solomon Pappaiah’s gloss stresses learning from the great as the start of that process. Vaaraa neri, ‘the path of no return’, closely echoes the Gita’s ‘one who reaches it never returns’. The formula reaches across traditions: Revelation’s ‘he shall go no more out’ and the Orphic initiate’s escape from the ‘circle’ of births voice the same idea of a final exit.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That abode of Mine is not illumined by the sun or moon, nor by electricity. One who reaches it never returns to this material world.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the supreme state as self-luminous and final: whoever reaches it is never born into this world again.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘vaaraa neri’ (the path that does not come back) is almost a translation of the Gita’s ‘never returns’.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on the no-return destination; the Gita frames it as reaching Krishna’s abode, the Kural as seeing the True.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out.”
christianity.explanation: The risen Christ promises that the faithful will be made permanent in God’s presence and will never be sent away again.
christianity.tie_back: A final, irreversible arrival parallels the Kural’s path of no return.
christianity._accuracy_note: Moderate: permanence and no leaving, but Christianity has no cycle of rebirth to escape, and the means is faithfulness rather than insight.

islam.quote_or_event: “Wherein they abide eternally. They will not desire from it any transfer.”
islam.explanation: Speaking of the gardens of Paradise, the Qur’an says their dwellers remain forever and never wish to leave.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ‘vaaraa neri’, the destination is final: no departure and no return to the former state.
islam._accuracy_note: Finality matches; Islam has no rebirth cycle, and entry is by faith and righteous deeds (18:107), not by knowledge alone.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Jacob said: this world is like a vestibule before the world to come; prepare yourself in the vestibule, so that you may enter the banqueting-hall.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah teaches that this life is an entrance hall where one prepares (through Torah study and good deeds) to enter the lasting world to come.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘kattru eendu’ (having learned here) likewise treats this life as the place where one prepares for the final destination.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on ‘prepare here for what lies beyond’; lacks the no-return/rebirth dimension.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who has reached the goal, is fearless, free from craving, passionless, and has plucked out the thorns of existence — for him this is the last body.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says the one who has fully realized the goal will never take another body: this life is their last.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘matreendu vaaraa’ (never coming here again) is the Buddhist ‘last body’.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very strong match on liberation in this life ending rebirth.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Gold leaves buried with Orphic-Bacchic initiates in southern Italy (4th century BCE) have the dead person declare to the underworld queen that they are pure and have escaped the grievous, weary circle, hoping to become a god instead of a mortal.
greek_mythology.explanation: Initiates believed that sacred knowledge and purification let the soul break out of the cycle of births for good.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Striking parallel: a Greek belief that knowledge and purity end the ‘circle’ of rebirth, the Kural’s path of no return.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; translations of the tablets vary and the texts are fragmentary. Mystery-religion rather than mainstream Olympian myth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the closing myth of the Phaedo, Socrates says that those who have sufficiently purified themselves through philosophy live thereafter entirely without bodies and reach dwellings fairer still.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato’s Socrates, the true philosopher’s lifelong pursuit of wisdom ends in the soul’s release from the cycle of embodiment.
philosophy.tie_back: The same sequence as the Kural: learning and seeing the truth in this life leads to not coming back into a body.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong structural match (philosophy → no re-embodiment), given in the form of a myth.

kurals.tamil:
ஓர்த்துள்ளம் உள்ளது உணரின் ஒருதலையாப்
பேர்த்துள்ள வேண்டா பிறப்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Orththullam ulladhu unarin orudhalaiyaap
Perththulla vendaa pirappu.
kurals.meaning: If the mind has carefully examined and firmly grasped That Which Truly Is, there is no need to think of being born again.
kurals.elementary: Once you truly understand that the monster under the bed was only a shadow, you don’t have to be scared of it again tomorrow night. This kural says that once your mind really and firmly understands what is real, you don’t have to worry about coming back to be born again.
kurals.university: Ulladhu, literally ‘that which is’, is one of the most philosophically loaded words in the chapter. It corresponds to the Sanskrit sat (Being) and later gave its name to Ramana Maharshi’s Tamil work Ulladhu Narpadhu (‘Forty Verses on That Which Is’). Orththu (having reflected or investigated) and oru-thalaiyaa (with complete, one-pointed certainty) spell out the method: truth is reached by sustained inquiry until conviction is total. Traditional glosses (Solomon Pappaiah speaks of holding fully in mind ‘what was heard from the great’) connect this to the Vedantic sequence of hearing, reflection and contemplation (shravana, manana, nididhyasana). The language of ‘what is’ invites comparison with Parmenides, for whom Being is ‘uncreated and indestructible’, and with Maimonides, for whom knowing the Primary Being is ‘the foundation of all foundations’. Valluvar’s distinctive claim is soteriological: to grasp Being is to end becoming.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The fetter of the heart is broken, all doubts are solved, all his works (and their effects) perish when He has been beheld who is high and low.”
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad says that when the ultimate Reality is directly seen, every bond, every doubt, and all karma that would cause future births fall away.
hinduism.tie_back: Just as the Kural says, firm realization of ‘ulladhu’ removes the karmic cause of rebirth; the same Upanishad describes aiming the mind ‘at that which is’.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match: certainty (doubts solved) + end of karmic consequence; rebirth is implied through ‘works perish’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.”
christianity.explanation: In his prayer before his arrest, Jesus defines eternal life itself as knowing the one true God.
christianity.tie_back: Both teach that knowing the ultimate Reality is itself the deathless state.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close in making knowledge of the True the essence of salvation; relational knowledge of a personal God, not rebirth-ending insight.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who remember Allāh while standing or sitting or [lying] on their sides and give thought to the creation of the heavens and the earth, [saying], ‘Our Lord, You did not create this aimlessly; exalted are You [above such a thing]; then protect us from the punishment of the Fire.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises those who reflect deeply on creation, reach certainty of its purpose and its Creator, and so seek salvation.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ‘orththu’ (having reflected), careful contemplation leads to grasping the Real and being saved from a dreaded fate.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on reflection → knowledge → salvation; the feared fate is the Fire, not rebirth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The foundation of all foundations and the pillar of wisdom is to know that there is a Primary Being who brought into being all existence.”
judaism.explanation: Maimonides opens his code of Jewish law by making knowledge of the one true Being, from whose truth everything exists, the first commandment and the basis of wisdom.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘ulladhu’ (That Which Is) and Maimonides’s ‘Primary Being’ both place knowing true Being at the summit of wisdom.
judaism.source: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:1 (trans. Eliyahu Touger)
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on ‘knowing Being’; no link to escaping rebirth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is, monks, an unborn — unbecome — unmade — unfabricated. If there were not that unborn — unbecome — unmade — unfabricated, there would not be the case that escape from the born — become — made — fabricated would be discerned.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha affirms that there really is an unborn, unconditioned reality, and that because it exists, escape from birth is possible.
buddhism.tie_back: Echoes the Kural’s logic: realizing what truly ‘is’ (the unborn) removes the need to be born again.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close conceptually; Buddhism avoids calling Nibbana ‘Being’ in the Vedantic sense.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Myth of Er, souls about to be reborn must drink from the River of Unmindfulness (Lethe) on the Plain of Forgetfulness. Those not protected by wisdom drink more than the measure and forget everything before entering a new life.
greek_mythology.explanation: In this Greek picture of reincarnation, forgetting the truth goes hand in hand with being reborn; wisdom is what limits that forgetting.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Inverse parallel: in the Kural, firmly remembering and knowing the truth is what makes rebirth unnecessary.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. A philosophical myth rather than traditional mythology; wisdom reduces forgetfulness but does not end rebirth in the Er story.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “In this path are very many tokens that what is is uncreated and indestructible; for it is complete, immovable, and without end.”
philosophy.explanation: Parmenides argues that true Being (‘what is’) never comes into being or passes away; birth and death belong only to mortal opinion.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘ulladhu’ is Parmenides’s ‘what is’: to grasp the ungenerated is to stand outside birth.
philosophy.source: Parmenides, Fragment 8 (DK B8; trans. John Burnet)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Excellent terminological match on ‘what is’; Parmenides is doing logic and cosmology, not soteriology.

kurals.tamil:
பிறப்பென்னும் பேதைமை நீங்கச் சிறப்பென்னும்
செம்பொருள் காண்பது அறிவு.
kurals.transliteration:
Pirappennum pedhaimai neengach sirappennum
Semporul kaanpadhu arivu.
kurals.meaning: True wisdom is seeing the perfect Truth, called the Supreme Good, so that the folly called ‘birth’ is removed.
kurals.elementary: Imagine being stuck on a merry-go-round that never stops because you forgot there’s an exit. The moment you notice the exit sign, you can step off. This kural says being born again and again is like forgetting the exit, and seeing what is truly real is the exit sign.
kurals.university: The couplet makes a bold equation: pirappu ennum pedhaimai, ‘the folly called birth’. Birth is not only caused by ignorance (as in 351); it is itself named a form of ignorance. Against it stands sirappu ennum semporul, ‘the perfect Truth called excellence’, which commentators read as the Supreme Being or the state of release (Mu. Varadarasanar glosses sirappu as mukti). Semporul (‘the fine, perfect substance’) is the same term used in 359 for the support of all things. Buddhism offers the closest structural parallel: in dependent origination, ignorance (avijja) is the first condition and rebirth (jati) the eleventh, so the fading of ignorance ends birth. Hindu parallels such as Gita 4.9 make knowledge of the divine the reason one ‘does not take birth again’, while John’s ‘the truth shall make you free’ expresses liberation through knowing within a linear rather than cyclical cosmology.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who knows the transcendental nature of My appearance and activities does not, upon leaving the body, take his birth again in this material world, but attains My eternal abode, O Arjuna.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says that truly knowing the divine reality ends rebirth: at death such a knower goes to the eternal abode instead.
hinduism.tie_back: Just as the Kural says, seeing the supreme Truth (semporul) removes the ‘folly called birth’.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Direct match: knowledge of the Supreme → no rebirth. The Gita focuses on knowing Krishna, the Kural on the Truth in general.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that knowing the truth frees a person from bondage (in context, the bondage of sin).
christianity.tie_back: Same core claim as the Kural: seeing the Truth is what liberates.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on knowledge → freedom; the bondage in John is sin, not rebirth.

islam.quote_or_event: “That is because Allāh is the True Reality, and that which they call upon other than Him is falsehood, and because Allāh is the Most High, the Grand.”
islam.explanation: One of God’s names is al-Haqq, ‘the Truth’ or ‘the True Reality’. Everything else people cling to as ultimate is, by comparison, falsehood.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘semporul’ (the perfect Truth) corresponds closely to al-Haqq as the one Reality to be recognized.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on ‘God as the True Reality’; no concept of birth as ignorance.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth.”
judaism.explanation: Through Jeremiah, God says that the only thing worth boasting of is not wisdom, strength or riches but understanding and knowing Him (da’at).
judaism.tie_back: Both texts set knowledge of the ultimate Truth above every other kind of knowing.
judaism._accuracy_note: Matches the supremacy of knowing the divine; lacks the ‘birth as ignorance’ theme.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Ignorance is a requirement for choices. … Continued existence is a requirement for rebirth. … When ignorance fades away and ceases no residue left behind, choices cease. … When rebirth ceases, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress cease.”
buddhism.explanation: Dependent origination traces rebirth back, link by link, to ignorance; when ignorance ends completely, rebirth and all its suffering end too.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim spelled out step by step: birth is rooted in ignorance, and removing ignorance removes birth.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near-exact doctrinal match (ignorance → birth; end of ignorance → end of birth). Quoted with ellipses; wording verbatim from Sujato.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In a Greek legend, King Midas captured the satyr Silenus and asked what is best for mankind; Silenus answered that it is best never to be born, and next best to die soon. Sophocles’ chorus in Oedipus at Colonus echoes this: not to be born is best of all.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek tragic wisdom saw human birth itself as a misfortune.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s startling view of birth as something to be escaped, but offers no path of knowledge out of it.
greek_mythology.source: Sophocles, Oedipus at Colonus 1224–1227; Silenus legend
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; weak-to-moderate. Pessimism about birth matches, but there is no liberating ‘Truth’ or end to rebirth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plotinus urges the soul to withdraw from the world of images and ‘flee to the beloved Fatherland’, turning inward to behold the One, the source of all being, from which the soul came and to which it can return.
philosophy.explanation: For Plotinus, the soul’s descent into bodies is a kind of forgetting, and contemplative vision of the One reverses it.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, embodiment is tied to ignorance, and seeing the supreme Reality is the way home.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good structural match, though Plotinus’s ‘return’ is mystical union rather than an explicit end to reincarnation.

kurals.tamil:
சார்புணர்ந்து சார்பு கெடஒழுகின் மற்றழித்துச்
சார்தரா சார்தரு நோய்.
kurals.transliteration:
Saarbunarndhu saarbu keda ozhukin matrazhiththuch
Saardharaa saardharu noi.
kurals.meaning: Whoever understands the true Support of all things, and lives so that every lesser attachment falls away, will find that the sorrows that would have clung to them, destroying their efforts, cling no more.
kurals.elementary: If you’re holding a hundred balloons, the wind can drag you anywhere. But if you let go of them and hold on to one strong railing, you stay safe. This kural says: know what is truly worth holding on to, let the other things go, and troubles can’t grab hold of you.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on a remarkable pun: the root saar- (‘to lean on, cling to, attach’) appears four times: saarbu unarndhu (knowing the true support), saarbu keda (so that attachments perish), saardharaa (will not cling) and saardharu noi (the afflictions that would cling). Commentators read the first saarbu as the Supreme Truth (semporul), the support of all things, and the second as worldly attachment (pattru). The wordplay thus contrasts one legitimate ‘leaning’ with many illegitimate ones. The logic, that attachment is the channel through which suffering ‘attaches’, is shared with Buddhist teaching on upadana (grasping) and with the Gita’s call to cut the world-tree ‘with the weapon of detachment’ while taking refuge in its root. Islam’s divine name as-Samad, the One on whom all depend, offers an especially close lexical parallel to the first saarbu.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “But with determination one must cut down this tree with the weapon of detachment. So doing, one must seek that place from which, having once gone, one never returns, and there surrender to that Supreme Personality of Godhead from whom everything has begun and in whom everything is abiding since time immemorial.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna pictures worldly existence as a deep-rooted tree to be cut with detachment, while the seeker takes refuge in the Supreme in whom everything rests.
hinduism.tie_back: The same double movement as the Kural: cut false attachments (saarbu keda) and rest in the true Support of all (saarbu unarndhu).
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match of both halves: detachment + refuge in the ground of all being.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal … For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns against clinging to perishable possessions and tells his hearers to anchor their hearts in heaven instead.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, what we cling to decides whether loss and sorrow can reach us.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on redirecting attachment; less explicit about suffering ceasing to ‘cling’.

islam.explanation: The Arabic as-Samad describes God as the One on whom all things depend and to whom everyone turns, while He depends on nothing.
islam.tie_back: As-Samad is a close equivalent of the Kural’s first ‘saarbu’, the true Support of all things, which the wise must recognize.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong lexical/conceptual match for ‘support of all’; the detachment half is not in this verse.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help. … Happy is he that hath the God of Jacob for his help, whose hope is in the LORD his God.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist warns against leaning on mortal powers that fail, and blesses the one whose support is God alone.
judaism.tie_back: Same contrast as the Kural: false supports that fail versus the one true Support.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match on true vs. false reliance; less focus on inner attachment.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From attachment springs grief, from attachment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from attachment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha traces grief and fear to attachment: remove the attachment and they have nothing to hold on to.
buddhism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s logic: when attachment perishes, the afflictions that would cling can no longer cling.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close on the attachment → suffering chain; Buddhism does not posit a ‘Support of all’ being.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Warned by Circe, Odysseus has his crew plug their ears with wax and has himself bound to the mast so that he can hear the Sirens’ song without being pulled to destruction by it.
greek_mythology.explanation: Knowing in advance what the lure really is, Odysseus holds fast to something firm and passes by the danger unharmed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, knowledge plus refusal to be seized by attraction keeps ruin from taking hold.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; a moderate allegorical fit. Odysseus still desires the song; he is restrained, not detached.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus opens his Handbook by dividing everything into what is up to us (our judgments, desires and aversions) and what is not (body, property, reputation), teaching that suffering comes from attaching ourselves to what is not ours.
philosophy.explanation: For the Stoics, clearly knowing what one’s good actually depends on, and detaching from everything else, makes a person unshakable.
philosophy.tie_back: Parallel to the Kural: know the true support, drop false dependencies, and misfortune can no longer grip you.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the Stoic ‘support’ is one’s own rational will, not a transcendent Being.

kurals.tamil:
காமம் வெகுளி மயக்கம் இவ்மூன்றன்
நாமம் கெடக்கெடும் நோய்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaamam vekuli mayakkam ivmoondran
Naamam kedakkedum noi.
kurals.meaning: When desire, anger and delusion (these three) are destroyed so completely that even their names are gone, the suffering they cause is destroyed too.
kurals.elementary: Weeds keep coming back if you only snip off the tops. You have to pull them out by the roots so nothing is left. This kural says greed, anger and confusion are like three weeds: pull them out so completely that even their names are forgotten, and the trouble they cause disappears.
kurals.university: The chapter closes by naming a triad: kaamam, vekuli, mayakkam (desire, anger, delusion). Its correspondence with the Buddhist ‘three roots’ or ‘three poisons’ (raga, dosa, moha: greed, hatred, delusion) is nearly exact, and it overlaps substantially with the Gita’s ‘three gates of hell’ (lust, anger, greed). Valluvar’s hyperbole, that the very names must perish (naamam keda), insists on eradication rather than suppression: not even the latent tendency or memory may remain. Because the chapter began with delusion (marul) as the cause of birth, ending with mayakkam as the third root closes the argument in a ring. True knowledge removes the delusion that fuels desire and anger, and with all three gone, the ‘disease’ (noi) of suffering and rebirth ends.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “There are three gates leading to this hell — lust, anger, and greed. Every sane man should give these up, for they lead to the degradation of the soul.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names three inner forces as the doorways to self-destruction and tells every sensible person to abandon them.
hinduism.tie_back: A near-parallel triad to the Kural’s kaamam–vekuli–mayakkam, with the same call to be rid of them completely.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close; the third member differs (greed in the Gita vs. delusion in the Kural).

christianity.quote_or_event: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world.”
christianity.explanation: John names a threefold root of worldly corruption, and says none of it comes from God.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, a triad of inner drives is identified as the source of spiritual sickness to be overcome.
christianity._accuracy_note: Parallel triadic structure; the members differ (no anger or delusion as such).

islam.quote_or_event: “But as for he who feared the position of his Lord and prevented the soul from [unlawful] inclination, then indeed, Paradise will be [his] refuge.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an promises Paradise to the one who holds back the lower self (nafs) from its passions.
islam.tie_back: Both texts make victory over passion the condition for escaping suffering.
islam._accuracy_note: General match on overcoming desire; no explicit triad, and the language is restraint rather than eradication.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Elazar Ha-kappar said: envy, lust and [the desire for] honor put a man out of the world.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah names three inner vices that destroy a person’s life in this world and the next.
judaism.tie_back: A striking triad parallel: three passions that ruin a person, which the Kural says must be destroyed down to their names.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close triadic structure; members differ partly (envy and honor vs. anger and delusion).

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Reverend, the ending of greed, hate, and delusion is called extinguishment.”
buddhism.explanation: Asked what Nibbana (extinguishment) is, Sariputta defines it simply as the ending of the three roots: greed, hate and delusion.
buddhism.tie_back: An almost exact match: the Kural’s kaamam–vekuli–mayakkam are the Buddhist raga–dosa–moha, and their destruction is liberation.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: same three members, same order, same claim that their ending is the end of suffering.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Heracles fought the Lernaean Hydra, each head he cut off grew back as two, until his companion Iolaus burned the stumps so that none could regrow; the immortal head was buried under a heavy rock.
greek_mythology.explanation: The monster could only be defeated by destroying it at the root so nothing could grow back.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ‘even the names must perish’, cutting off passions superficially fails; they must be destroyed at the source.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; allegorical fit only. The myth itself is not about inner passions.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza argues that a passion ceases to be a passion as soon as we form a clear and distinct idea of it, and that the more we understand our emotions, the less we are ruled by them.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, true understanding does not merely restrain destructive emotions; it dissolves them as passions.
philosophy.tie_back: Matches the chapter’s whole logic: knowledge of the truth is what destroys desire, anger and confusion at the root.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong match on knowledge dissolving passion. Spinoza has no triad and no rebirth.
